sections.text: Compound types group several values together. Rust has two built in: tuples and arrays.
A tuple groups a fixed number of values that can have different types. Get at the parts with .0, .1 and so on, or unpack them with let (this is called destructuring):
An array holds a fixed number of values that all have the same type. Count from 0 when you index it:
{:?} is debug formatting. It prints whole tuples and arrays, which plain {} can't.

Coming from another language: Rust never reads past the end of an array. If you write a fixed index that's too big, like days[10] on this 5-day array, the compiler spots it and refuses to build. If the index is only known while the program runs, it stops with an "index out of bounds" error. When you need a list that can grow, use a Vec (Unit 5).
The first item is at index 0, so the last item of a 5-item array is at index 4.
